observation_window.sampling: provider default; not continuous motion capture

extraction.teacher_style: The instructor breaks down complex musical phrasing and rhythms using apps and clear verbal explanations. He demonstrates steps in front of a mirror with step-by-step breakdowns.

lesson_structure.note: Guaguanco connecting basic steps & coordination to the rhythm
Introducing percussion app to isolate musical elements
Comparing rumba clave and son clave rhythms
Basic rumba step: press and step
Adding shekere and explaining opposite arm coordination

cues: opposite arm drives the upper body movement
common_mistakes: losing chest posture when bending knees
making side steps massive and messing up weight transfer
safety: bent knees and hinging forward at the hip so you don't lose your chest

steps_taught.name: Basic step in place
steps_taught.description: Press with one foot and step without full weight change on the press.

steps_taught.name: Side step
steps_taught.description: Step out to the side while maintaining the press and weight transfer rhythm.

steps_taught.name: Traveling forward/back
steps_taught.description: Applying the basic in-place press and weight transfer while moving forward and backward.

steps_taught.name: 3-step
steps_taught.description: Step under your center with movement happening on counts 2 and 3.

what_works: breaking down each percussion instrument separately
showing footwork close-ups alongside mirror demonstrations
what_hinders: rhythm and musicality explanations can feel complex for beginners

quotes.text: The body position you want is just bent knees and hinging forward at the hip.
That little hesitation is what makes rumba clave rumba clave.
That is a lifesaver if you're trying to find the beat.

evidence_segments.observation: Instructor demonstrates posture with bent knees and hinged hips facing the mirror.
Close-up of feet showing press and step weight transfer.

extraction.distinctive_method: Isolating each individual percussion instrument layer (clave, cata', shekere, tumba, tres-dos, quinto) and mapping specific body movements or weight transfers to each one before dancing.
